title: Old-time dances versus modern bands
summary: Mello says today's musicians cannot play the program of waltzes, lancers and mazurkas, and describes prize waltzes, rowdy late dances and 'rotten notes'.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I know, but today, the generation and the musicians that they have now will never, and you can take that from me as an authority, will never play the music we used to play in our days. For the simple reason is that they didn't, they gave you a program. All right, you play according to the program. Now, that program maybe might have contained 12, 14, or 16 different type dances. Mazzucca, lances, shatters, waltzes, minuets, varieties. That was all on the program, and you played just the way the program was. Show me if any of these fellas is Humpback. And you take in the old days when you got a, you got a, a dance, and you played at a ball, and you see these people dancing. Why? Why? It was a, a, a, something nice to look at. I had a friend of mine who was coming, Pansylane and I, Hookland better known as, who was coming from a layup one night, not a layup, but we went to a meet, and they had a dance on St. Croix and Ann and Roy. So, we came through there, and who was camped there, but Redhill, Lieutenant Redhill, and Louie Kenricks, police. And I says to Louie, I said, what you doing here? Well, he says, I'm learning how to dance. Redhill says, you don't have to know how to dance to dance, that dance. He says, all you got to do is get up and shake your tail, that's all. You're dancing. But which is the truth. Which is the truth. Now, you don't see them dance, you never seen them dance except after 12 o'clock, in places that was known, like the Perfect Union Hall, and back at the Unexpected, back at the Main Street, and the Tonti. Not much at the Tonti, but the Perfect Union on Rampart Street, which has Point Down, and the Unexpected back at the Main Street. You've seen some of that carrying on after 12 o'clock. That's when the rough gang got in. But you don't see, you never seen that in the regular dance. Go to look at the regular dance now and see what you can see. Just take a look at the regular dance now and see what you can see. It's a disgrace. And what I know, I know it to be a positive fact that the old days, these modern times will never revoit back to the old days, that they won't. But the dances will never be the same. Never will be the same. In the old days, you had good dances. And when you danced, and you played a waltz and you seen them dance a waltz, that was something nice to look at. Especially when they had a prize waltz and they chalked their heels. You never heard of that, did you? No. They had about eight or ten fellas on the floor, you know, and they'd be watching you in the prize court. They had good prizes. You put your foot down, find out what happens. You're marks there, you're gone. You're out. You had to dance on your toes all the time. But now, now it's a flat foot dance like the knees used to dance in the old days. So, that's the way the things are running now. Of course, I'm not condemning. Or am I not? I don't want it to be misconstrued that I'm knocking at the present age, or anything else. I'm not. But we just comparing the times, the old times and now. There's nothing more nicer to see than a dance. You go to a dancer that had real dances in. But now, what do you see? Oh, valley hood, wreck them up, bust up, leave one fella, blow his brains out one way and the other fella on the drum beat, and his brains out, what happens? Oh, that's beautiful music. You can't tell what they're playing. You can't. In my band, when I always tried to lead, if I led, let Martin Kurch do the dirty work of Yellow Nunes. If Martin Kurch led, he let me do the dirty work on the drum beat. And we had certain parts there that was just nice work, nice execution for the drum beat. But now what? One fella's trying to go above the staff. It's usurpation of music. That's what it is. You take orchestras from the violin on down. You take the violin, the clarinet, the cornet, the trumbo. You never had saxophone, see? But you never did hear the cornet try to outdo the clarinet. And you never heard the clarinet try to outdo the fiddle. Boy, he'd get out of some position on the fiddle and he'd make you sick. Now, did you ever hear of a mute for a fiddle? I have. You have? Sure. Shove it on a bridge? Yeah. Boy, that's fine, yeah. I played with them fellas. I played with one or two fellas that really could use a mute. And you could play that. They don't absorb the signs in music. Ain't no such thing as canister. It's double 40. Double 40 all the way through. They start off 40 and they end up on double 40. Come right back to double 40. They hit adult single-sided going on right back. No matter if they got one P on the staff or two Ps, they disregard that. See, they're looking at the two Fs. So, we used to... We... I'll say this and I'll say it again. Popeye Lane's living, he'll tell you. We used to play that soft, but you can hear their feet on the floor. You hear that now? Not unless they put sand on their shoes. That's out. I listen to quite a few bands and I hear quite a few fellas say, Oh, I can lay in bed. Music loves me to sleep. Not me. I listen for the rotten notes they make. That's what I do. I listen for the rotten notes. Long before I was married there, we used to have the Nemo Club on Congress in Burgundy. We used to have dances there for the regular anyhow twice a week. We played that quite a few times. And we'd come in maybe from playing our job and they'd have one or two badges to come there. Nigger in there and somebody else. Boy, that was the smell of the band. And Leon said, Leon said, Leon said, Leon said, Leon on that side and I'd be laying on this side in the other room. And I said, Whoa, whoa. Said, you smell that? Rotten notes. Of course, people didn't know it. But that was my trouble. I can lay in this bed right now and hear a band playing. And I don't, uh, I would sleep. I couldn't sleep. Because I wait for the next mother to make a rotten note. A rotten stop or rotten something else. I'll tell you what I do. I like music. I can sit down and talk music all day, all night, and all day. I like music. But I don't like music like they play it now. Here's another thing. You can look for this. Lawrence Welk has a dissension in his band. When he put a half a million more strings in there, and he's got one or two others, that's instead of having in the trumpet section two solos and two poets, you've got them all playing solo. Which is wrong. Anyhow, in a band of each size. He's got a couple of these men quit. But, uh, I told my wife that Saturday a week ago. I says, you know something? She says, what? I said, Lawrence Welk's got a dissension in his band. And I'm the boy who can see it. I'm the boy who can see it. Of course, after you play music as long as I play it, you know when the dissension's starting and when it's not. You can see it. Especially when you get four trumpets working together and then one fella try to outgrow the other and make the most noise and every other present thing. Well, I have one. You want to smoke? Go ahead and hug yourself.
